item.title: Apple is adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — without new hardware
item.description:
Apple is working on a face unlock feature for the iPhone Duo that uses the front-facing camera for authentication, and it's already testing it with the new iOS 27.3 beta released today, as reported by MacRumors. The iPhone Duo's face unlock feature seemingly has a few caveats, however: it's only available for the lock screen, you can only use your face for an unlock if you have used Touch ID or input a passcode within 45 minutes …

item.title: Nvidia’s board is reportedly ‘not considering’ hiring Jensen Huang back
item.description:
Nvidia's board of directors "isn't considering" having Jensen Huang return as CEO, according to a report from CNBC. A source tells the outlet the board "is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back."

item.title: 15 hotel guests were injured by chlorine poisoning due to Microsoft’s global email outage
item.description:
Microsoft's worldwide 365 and Outlook outage had real-world consequences after it cut off email alerts for a German hotel's pool safety system. The German outlet Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR) said several people were injured at a Phantasialand hotel on Friday after its email system failed to deliver a safety alert about elevated chlorine levels in the pool, as spotted earlier by NotebookCheck and TechRadar.

A machine-translated Facebook post from a German fire department said it responded to a Phantasialand hotel after a "technical malfunction" caused an excessive amount of chlorine to enter a swimming pool, resulting in chlorine gas leaking …

item.title: Why NJ’s governor thinks Republicans are trapped in an X bubble
item.description:
Today I’m talking with Mikie Sherrill, who’s been New Jersey governor for just a little under a year, and you’ll hear her say her election was a preview of the huge Democratic victories in these recent midterms because she ran on the dual themes of affordability and accountability.

So I wanted to ask the governor exactly how corruption became such an animating issue for voters, in an era of tech billionaires who own platforms like X and TikTok and who also now control huge swaths of local media and even national broadcast media like CBS News.

You’ll hear us get into the new era of influencer politics, which plays out as social video and takes its cues from rising stars like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and how I think influence on platforms like Elon Musk’s X is starting to backfire in big ways for conservatives.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

But the real story this election cycle might be the states. With President Donald Trump concentrating power in the executive branch, governors like Sherrill are starting to exercise their own power in ways that haven’t been tested in a long time.

This runs right into tech policy and anti-AI backlash, as states around the country try to address topics like child safety and Big Tech overreach in lieu of any form of meaningful federal regulation. That’s how politicians like Sherrill have found themselves at the forefront of the data center fight, online privacy, and age verification — all topics you’ll hear us dive into here.

We also dig into the Meta settlement, why Sherrill expects more Big Tech litigation, and what happens to privacy in the Flock and AI era. She had a lot of questions about the last one, and honestly, so do I. It’s a conversation I think we’re all going to be having for a while.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Governor Mikie Sherrill, you’re the governor of New Jersey. Welcome to Decoder.

Well, thanks so much for having me. I really appreciate it.

I’m excited to talk to you. It’s after the midterms; there’s a huge blue wave, and you’re a Democrat.

I noticed.

Yeah. I noticed that you were saying, “New Jersey is like the bellwether,” and you “paved the way…” This is your big quote. Tell me about that, and tell me how you’re feeling about the midterms.

I’ll answer the easy question first. I feel great about the midterms. I feel absolutely fantastic about the midterms. And yeah, I was thinking about it because New Jersey has those off-year elections. So, there are very few statewide races — really only two in that cycle: New Jersey and Virginia. Right after Trump won, we started our campaign. And by right after, I mean, he won in November of 2024, and we started our campaign in November of 2024. What’s so interesting about New Jersey is that, even for a governor of this state, it’s still so retail. I don’t think a lot of other big states do as much retail, meaning I’m getting in front of thousands and thousands of people, sometimes per day, at small business stops, at diners, in their community… We have so many municipalities. I am able to go to gatherings of people up and down my state.

And that means that we always have a real pulse on what’s going on very quickly. After 2024, we had to get the vibe because it was different; people were furious. They wanted movement, they wanted change, and then suddenly you have Elon Musk with a chainsaw. People are scared, they don’t like what’s happening, and they want a leader who’s going to address it. And I think what we did in that time, because we heard from everyone, is really centered on what the race was about, and it was about affordability and accountability.

I know now that seems obvious… Yeah, it’s about affordability, and everyone knows that. I don’t think it was obvious in 2024 what it was all about. What was driving people? And in New Jersey, we were able to figure that out, and I think because the campaign was so incredibly successful, and we had such a huge win at the end of the day, that people then thought, oh yeah, that’s exactly the path. We’re all going to run on affordability and accountability, and that’s powerful in the Democratic Party. I think we’re at the center of our power when we’re fighting for working families, and that’s where we are right now, and I think it bodes really well for the future.

One of the really surprising aspects of this last election cycle was corruption leading the polls in several places. You don’t often see people on CNBC being like, “Our poll says corruption is the number one issue in America.” I think it was number two in The Guardian poll. I feel like I can connect corruption to all the tech CEOs being at the White House all the time, and to data centers. Is that a real connection, or is that just because I happen to live in the tech bubble?

So, as somebody who has worked with polling, good, bad, and everything in between, I would say, and not to sound like a broken record, we were talking about… And that corruption piece was part of the accountability, the affordability. And I was hearing about that anger at corruption on the trail, even from very small, modest businesses, tying it to Trump pocketing billions of dollars as their costs are going up. I think you’re exactly right. People are very upset at the tech billionaires, and when they’re hanging out at the White House, especially those flip-floppers. They’re all in on liberal values, and then they’re all in on Trump values. It’s just to make a buck. The reason corruption popped so much is people… It’s not just corruption; it’s the corruption that’s costing them money.

It’s Trump going into this Iranian war that he can’t explain and somehow making billions of dollars. It’s Trump trying to allow Russian diesel here, as everyone else is paying higher and higher gas prices, and everyone knows that Russia is funding Iran. And oh, by the way, the oligarchs are funding the wedding of Trump’s kid. Just so much corruption, and it’s tied, I think, specifically, to people’s ideas of their pocketbook and what’s making this go up. Everyone thinks it’s because Trump’s partly on the take here.

One of the things that I’ve been really thinking about is how people found out about the corruption, how they talked to each other about it, and why it became such an issue. And the reason I’m asking that way is, well, Elon Musk owns X, right? He bought a social media network. Larry Ellison and Oracle have some controlling stake in TikTok. Mark Zuckerberg owns Instagram. Skydance exists, and it owns CNN. The idea that the tech billionaires control the media, and have bought more and more of the media, was supposed to create even more of an epistemic bubble. We are going to tweet policy into reality is as much a part of Trump Two as anything, and people found out what they wanted to find out, and yet they had these conversations. I haven’t been able to figure out why; do you have a theory about that case?

There was a lot of corruption that we were trying to bring to the fore that was really hard to have people connect with. I think, for example, when we had Congress block some of the most high-end semiconductor chips so that we could win some of the technological battle against China, and Trump basically got paid off by the UAE, and then suddenly the floodgates were open. So, we had seen all of this cryptocurrency and stuff going into his pocketbooks. I suspect there’s a lot we don’t even know. But your point is really a good one because we were sort of saying he’s corrupt, and people sort of felt that he was corrupt, but the specifics of it were hard to bring out or get into the public consciousness. I tend to think that the interesting thing is… And look, I was very worried. I first ran in 2018, and I started to see the misinformation that people were getting online, and how people were getting algorithms driving them into more and more extreme places.

I was quite skeptical of some of this new media and what it might mean for people getting information. That is certainly one concern, but the flip side of that has become, as people have gotten used to some of that extremism and maybe started to filter it out a little bit, that there’s not much you can hide now, and I think that’s really good for democracy. So, for example, we had a problem here with our voter rolls. We discovered that the last administration had registered people who were not citizens, and they had not cleared them off the rolls. And so, we discovered this, and there were a lot of people saying, “Just put out a paragraph and just kind of duck and cover and hope it goes away. Sweep it under the rug a little bit.” And to me, that’s not accountability, that’s not what I ran on, and that’s not being a strong leader. Being a strong leader is saying, “Yeah, a problem happened, but I’ve got the solution to it, and I’m going to handle it.” And I think that breeds trust in government.

The reason that I maybe felt so strongly about this was that there’s no sweeping things under the rug in that way, and I think that’s really healthy. Meaning that if I had just put a little paragraph out, then the narrative would’ve gotten out anyway. I wouldn’t have been able to tell people exactly what happened, why it happened, and what we were doing about it; it would’ve been put out in whatever way somebody else wanted it out there. And so, I think what some people aren’t realizing is: you can’t hide much from the American people. The best thing you can do, and I think this is also my view of democracy and good government, is to be accountable to people. And to come forward strongly and say, this is what happened, this is why it happened, this is how I’m fixing it.

One of the things that I’m really curious about in that construction is how much of this cycle was dominated by politicians who had essentially learned the visual and social vernacular of influencers. And Zohran Mamdani here in New York City has obviously learned how to wield social media as well as any influencer. Abdul El-Sayed has learned that language. After the election, I think it was a House Oversight Committee that released what can only be described as an NBA hype reel with just the words “lawyer up” over and over again.

And there’s a part of me that’s like, this is incredibly effective. This is also a totally new brand of… Chuck Schumer should not do that. He doesn’t know how to do that. You need a new generation of politicians who speak this language, and sort of wield the algorithms against their owners in a very specific way. Do you think that’s permanent? Is that just a moment in time, or is influencer politics here to stay?

I think getting out on social media and being very present there feels very permanent to me. There certainly are people who do it incredibly well. But the interesting thing to me is that it’s not replicable because I think you have to be so authentic. And so, Zohran Mamdani is gifted; he’s like a social media prodigy. I think he does a great job. Don’t I wish, right? I think part of the reason I like what he does is that he comes across with a lot of humanity, a lot of empathy for people, reaching out to all different kinds of people, and it’s New York City, and it feels very authentic.

But I also like that empathy piece. I think some people take from the more bravado and maybe the Oversight Committee, this idea that social media has to be real… I mean, just that you have to be kind of an asshole, and you have to get out there, and that’s how you get attention, and you’re just… And I see some people trying to do that. Look, I was in the Navy, and sometimes I curse like a sailor. I do not like to do that online. Kids are online; I’m a mom too, and I’m the governor of the state of New Jersey, so I don’t have to be crass online. I have to have, I think, some respect for the office. And there are some people who I don’t think actually use salty language in back rooms, but somehow think that if they start dropping F-bombs online, they’re going to be seen as tough on stuff.

The performative nature for some people is, I think, what gets them in trouble, and I think if you are authentic… And look, I’m going to be frank here, and I’m sorry, I’m not going to have as many followers as Zohran Mamdani. I’m just not. He’s, like I said, a prodigy, or gifted. I’m going to get the information; I’m going to connect with people. There are times when things hit, because we do so much in New Jersey, and people love New Jersey, and so we have a lot of Jersey stuff we do, and people like it. Great. People here in New Jersey are addicted to the weather. Great. We sadly have a lot of weather events, so we’ll hype it up. But at the same time, I think it’s really important to connect in an authentic way. And I think sometimes what you’ve seen is people looking at influencers or others who are good, and I think during the Trump administration, there were a lot of, quite frankly, toxic male bros, and somehow they learned this lesson. And yet, as you look across the people that just won, like Talarico, Amy Acton, Rob Sand… They were great people. They were really great people.

And I think those are the things that, when they come across, can be so powerful. I tend to think some of those people aren’t going to have Mamdani’s following either, but you have to be making sure that you’re talking to your electorate, and you’re the person that they elected you to be. That might have been a little rambling, but I think a lot about how you connect with people in an authentic way.

I’m really curious about that connection between policy, results, and authenticity. I think with Mayor Mamdani, you can see that he’s always trying to connect the policy to the result, and he’s obviously, like you said, very gifted at it. I’ll also say, I think that Rob Sand victory video, where he recreated the Fleetwood Mac meme with the cranberry juice, is an all-time piece of political communication. I’m not sure what it communicated, other than it ruled, but there is-

Sometimes you just love it. What was the one from the Mississippi senator? “Pick another protein.” I thought that was so good.

Yeah, it was very good. But there’s a vernacular there, right? It’s a video vernacular. In the history of politics, like JFK is the television president, there’s a vernacular with social video that came out in this election. And I’m really glad you brought up the sort of toxic energy of the Trump bros, because they feel like an X… They’re Twitter people, and they do barbs on Twitter-

Interesting. And you’re feeling like the newer ones are on, what do you say, Instagram? Is that-

Yeah, they’re on Instagram; they’re video. They’re natively video in a very particular way.

Right. I mean, X just feels toxic.

There’s something there.

Especially once Elon took it over, right?

Actually, here’s my hottest take. I’m curious if you agree with this.

Okay, yeah, I want to hear it.

My hottest take is that this election proved that Elon’s purchase of Twitter was a failure across every dimension.

Anytime you’re saying something proved Elon Musk’s something something was a failure, I’m here for you. I’m here for your hot take.

Well, it’s smaller than it used to be; he’s lost users. He is not making more money than Twitter ever did. And by the way, I want to qualify this by saying criticism of Elon Musk’s Twitter is in no way praise of the previous Twitter ownership. This thing has always been a disaster. But it’s smaller than it used to be; it’s certainly not making more money, and it has lost its political influence. I don’t think Twitter or X drives the national political conversation the way it used to. And in fact, because it’s become a bubble, I think it has confused a bunch of Republican politicians. I think it has confused the tech industry.

I’m wondering if you see that, right? You’re talking about how we’re in bubbles, and there’s more fragmentation, that you have to be more transparent, but I’m wondering if you see the sort of collapse of X in terms of its political influence.

So, you know I’m biased, but I think this is just another reason New Jersey kind of gets it right, because there are so many people who are saying they were astroturfed. I had to learn a new term in my campaign: astroturf, meaning they thought it was grassroots, but it was really just kind of the turf. There’s this fake energy sometimes on social media that people think is where everyone is at, and you can sometimes, as a good candidate in a campaign, really create that sense that everybody agrees in some area, or build a group that is going to really push that online. And yet, if you are on the ground speaking to real people all the time, you can get a sense of whether or not social media is matching up with where people are actually at.

I think time and time again, there is a sense that what is going on, especially, I would say on X, can give you this false sense of a bubble, and a false sense of where people are at. And the interesting thing… I think moving away from X can maybe change a little bit of this. I do think a lot of reporters would… It’s just easy. It’s easy to go through X and get the little blah, blah, blah and say, “This is what’s happening.” And you can really miss a lot of what’s going on if that’s… So, yes, I think the bubble can really fool people.

What did you make of the JD Vance post on X distancing himself from Trump, blaming it all on the war, and then the Hegseth video where he said, “Go ahead and try to impeach me.” Because those feel like pure X, like they’re talking to one audience in a small place. What’d you make of them?

If he wants to be impeached, I’m sure he can find somebody to do it. Yeah, let’s do it, let’s go. I think that bravado feels so 2024, and when you see the young men, especially, who I think were captured in… People felt like they were really in the movement, in the MAGA movement in 2024. As they are graduating, as they aren’t seeing any jobs, as they’re realizing they’re not going to be able to afford a house for many, many years, or even to be able to move out of their parents’ house, I think you are seeing a real swing away. Like it’s all fun and good if you’re at some loud rally where there’s a lot of music playing and you can be a tough guy, and you feel like that’s your team, like a sports event, but it’s not so fun and funny when you can’t get a job.

And so, that feels almost very 2024 to me and kind of missing the moment. That’s what’s so interesting about social media too. I think it moves very quickly. So, you might be the darling of whatever movement you’re in, and a couple years later you sound very tone-deaf.

I have one more question about the election and what it means. And I want to talk about New Jersey more specifically.

Trump Two has really been dominated by an almost anti-federalism. He tried to centralize a lot of power in the federal government, and the first AI bill the House passed was a 10-year moratorium on any state-level AI policy. There was a lot of, “We’re going to take power at the federal level. We’re going to bribe the states in various ways or punish the states if they don’t do what we say.” Now you’ve got a lot of democratic power across the whole government, in a bunch of state houses, in the federal government.

Do you think that’s going to swing back? Do you think we’re going to see more state-level policy? Do you think we’ll see more unification between what’s happening in all the democratic states and in Congress, or do you think we’ll see more experimentation?

I was listening to a political science person suggest that because of the way the US government is set up, there’s always going to be power that moves into a vacuum. And so, you saw the president taking all this power at the federal level; Congress was totally co-opted, and he had the presidency, the cabinet, and then he had the courts. So, you really did see the power moving to the people, and you started to see the people really engage more, as led by the states. In some of the governors’ offices and the state legislatures, that’s where power started to move to stand against what Trump was doing.

So I was so excited about Gina Hinojosa down in Texas. The biggest swing in my race was the Latino vote. I mean, we’re talking 18/22 points, which was a real precursor to some of that swing with the Latino vote in the other states in 2024. I just started looking around. Look, everybody’s talking about Talarico, so he’s bringing tons of people to the polls, and you have Bobby Polito, Johnny Garcia. I mean, you were seeing huge movements in their districts. Then Gina was saying, “Look, we have fielded congressional candidates in every race across the state, and so that’s going to bring people out.” I was just like, I think Gina’s got a great shot here. So, we did this big event for her three weeks before the race. Just thinking, we’ve got to get her some support here because I think she can do it.

And the reason I was so excited is, if you think about it, if we have California and the California governor, the Texas governor, and we have the New York governor… Man, we have a lot of the economy of the United States of America, and we can do a lot. We are moving into the state power.

So, for example, Trump said he was going to purchase Russian diesel. He has Russian diesel coming here. Now, I can’t tell you how opposed I am to that.

Right, you wanted to block it at the Port Authority [of New York and New Jersey], right?

Right, because they said they were coming to New Jersey. So, Russia is against Ukraine. I’m very opposed to their war against Ukraine. They are also supporting Iran, which we are currently at war with. I’m very opposed to the Iranian war, but they are killing Americans because we’re at war with them, and Russia is funding them. I mean, how can you, as the President of the United States of America, be putting money into the coffers of Russia? It is not acceptable on every single level, and it, oh, by the way, is illegal, because of laws that Congress has passed. I said, “It’s not coming into New Jersey.” But the states don’t traditionally have a lot of power here.

What we did was put every port and every business on notice in New Jersey that it was illegal. We charted out why it was illegal, and what laws Congress had passed, why what Trump and Bessent said was wrong — they were wrong on the law — and then we reminded everyone that the statute of limitations runs for five years, so don’t count on not getting caught on this one. And so far, we’ve seen a couple of ships turn away; I think we’re hearing that people are becoming very concerned about this, and not interested in it.

If somebody had told you that the state of New Jersey could turn back the president from importing oil into this country, you would’ve been skeptical, but that’s the kind of power states are moving into at the moment and using every tool we have. It’s not that we don’t have tools; it’s just that it’s a muscle that hasn’t been exercised in this way in a long time.

So, if we look to Texas, California, New York, along with New Jersey and other states, and there’s a bunch of Democratic ones now, if we want to — and we do — protect people from the downside risks of AI, we don’t need the federal government to do that. We can act as states. We can move in these ways that I think are very powerful, and have just become, after Tuesday, a lot more powerful.

Yeah, I’m fascinated by this dynamic.

Me too.

Especially with a heavily Democratic Congress, but then President Trump, who is threatening to veto everything. Some balance of power will shift to the states in some meaningful, potentially long-lasting way. It’s unclear exactly how that will work, but I think it will probably be the long-lasting story of this cycle.

I want to ask about New Jersey then, in that context. A year, not even a year into your first term, I think state governments are very opaque to people. I think a lot of the Decoder audience could tell you every bit of Apple’s org chart, and what the CO was, and what they do, and where the supply chain is, and they have no idea how their state government works.

So, I want to ask you the basic Decoder questions just to illuminate that a little bit. How is New Jersey structured? How have you structured your administration?

We have structured it differently than New Jersey has ever been structured. We are a large economy; we’d be the 22nd largest economy in the world if we were a country, and yet Trenton has not operated in that way. We added a chief operating officer. So, the top three people under me, my sort of lieutenants, if you will, are the chief of staff, and that’s a very traditional role. That’s sort of the person that works on the politics of the legislature and getting legislation passed… And I’m making these faces because I served in a legislature. Sometimes you have to muscle things through legislatures, even when you’re in them. You’ve got to get the coalitions; you’ve got to kind of arm-twist to get people there. In fact, the vote getter in a legislature is called the whip, to whip people into shape, to get them to vote on your bill.

That’s what the chief of staff does. She also works with the outside groups, and the grassroots groups, and the politics of it… Because if you are going to get people in your state to support legislation, you have to go communicate with them, and that’s politics, that’s getting in front of mayors and county commissioners, and talking about what this is going to do for their towns, and why it’s important. So, that’s the chief of staff.

Then you have the chief counsel. Now, the chief counsel sort of looks at the legislation and makes sure it’s constitutional. Are there any technical fixes that need to happen? Or are we going to get involved as a state in some of the different state legislation, like the Meta settlement and stuff? Are we going to take on some of these challenges? So, that’s sort of your chief counsel. And then we’ve added a third person, the chief operating officer.

The reason we added this person is that we just felt like the state wasn’t operating on… I come from the Navy, so on mission, meaning there were a lot of different cabinet departments, and you think of that as the federal level. So, you have the Department of Human Services, the Department of Health, the Department of Education, the Department of Transportation… I mean, what you would expect at the state level. And yet they all seem to be very siloed. They were experts operating in certain areas to do things, but if you’re going to do permitting reform, that’s going to touch on your Department of Community Affairs, your Department of Environmental Protection, your Department of Transportation. That is not a single sector; that crosses your different departments. So, your cabinet department. That is why we have the chief operating officer. She sort of brings everyone on mission, brings the cabinet together, and makes sure they’re all driving what we need to do.

Another thing that I think I have felt for a very long time, not just in New Jersey but across the board, is that the government just hasn’t been listening as well as it could, or serving people as well as it could. Running a good government hasn’t been appreciated for a very long time, and I wanted to make sure our government was delivering for people. So, when people were working on outdated systems like Cobalt, believe it or not… And yes, I’m not making that up. We were getting those systems up to date. When permits were too hard, and you had paper permits that everyone had to turn in across different departments, we were getting them online. When you have microfiche… Yes, microfiche. I’m old enough to have used it in the library; I’m sure a lot of people aren’t. Making sure we’re transferring that so that we’re getting the government to run well and then serve people better.

The other Decoder question I ask everybody is about decisions: how do you make decisions? What’s your framework?

I think it’s really critically important to just make decisions on a thing. And in politics, it’s often that if you’re just doing things for politics, not for policy or to deliver, it’s better not to make a decision. That’s kind of the dirty secret that has led to, I think, some government not serving people well. It’s often better to just stand back. I don’t know if you’ve seen that Homer Simpson one, where he goes into the tree? That’s what a lot of politicians seem to want to do, right? It’s just, “Whoa, that’s a tough one. That’s not popular, that’s not a good one; I’m going to let somebody else handle it.” And then when the decision is made, if it’s a good one, they’ll be like, “I supported that from the start.” So, I’ve raised my hand to be governor because it is my job to lead in tough things and to make tough decisions.

I center that work and making decisions on the people I serve. That is why, again, just being able to get in front of thousands of people helps me understand where people are so I can make decisions knowing how it’s going to impact people in my state, and then going back and checking in with people. And that’s why it’s so important to me how I run this government, so we can get the feedback loops. I like a lot of information, but if you’re going to onboard a lot of information, it has to come to you very particularly because of the human brain. So, you have to have systems in place so you can get as much information as possible, and make those decisions based on this information.

I have fantastic, fantastic people that work in Trenton. I think we have the most talent of any state government in the country, and so we have these feedback loops so I can make decisions. But part of the reason I’m able to do that, to get a lot of great information and to make these decisions, is because I trust the people who work for me. They’re that good, so I know when they’re giving me this information and their point of view, I can trust them and say, “Okay, that makes sense.” Because you’re sometimes doing things you don’t want to, and there are a lot of hard decisions you have to make.

You have to trust the people saying, “We’ve looked at every single path forward here, here, and here; we would pick here.” And you don’t feel like they’re leaving a lot out, or haven’t looked at it, or haven’t researched it well.

I want to put that all into practice, and I want to start with data centers. I really want to talk about the social media bills you have passed in the Meta lawsuit you mentioned, because the trade-offs there are as difficult as they get. But let’s start with data centers and AI for one second. You mentioned permitting. New Jersey’s an energy state; there’s a reason gas is flowing to New Jersey’s ports, that the big energy plants are there, the refiners are there. You announced a data center plan in May. You signed some bills in August related to build-outs; you were early to some of this backlash. You’ve got pillars here, right? You want water transparency, and you want them to bring their own power.

Do you think that these moratoriums, if they passed at all, are going to result in an outcome where the data centers get built, and people are happy about them? Or do you think that big tech companies and the people wanting to build these data centers need to start all the way over, and come up with a new plan?

Maybe a little bit of both. I don’t think a lot of people know all the different kinds of data centers or what it might mean to their community. We have local control here in New Jersey, so towns make their own decisions. And in some communities, data centers probably don’t make sense. But then there are other communities that have big industrial parks and big warehouse areas, away from where people live, that would make sense. But we want to make sure they’re not harming the communities — that they’re not utilizing too much water or driving up power costs. So, yes, we put in pillars to hold those data centers accountable. And for example, one of the data centers in the South that had been built before I got into office was not really following our different permitting laws and stuff. We’ve given one of the largest fines to them in the country — over a million dollars in fines — to hold them accountable.

We continue to work with communities. We’ve said we’ll have their back if they’re negotiating community benefits agreements, because what we want to make sure is that if a community goes forward with a data center, that it benefits the community and doesn’t just send billions of dollars to Big Tech in Silicon Valley. And what does that look like? That looks like ensuring that, with a community benefits agreement, they’re investing in the town. Some of the money being made there gets into the town and helps people. That they’re employing people, use good union labor, and stuff like that. And we’re not super scalers; we’re not building some of what you see out in Texas, but people do want to have more insight into it.

The reason I say a little bit of both is because I don’t think data centers have shown a model where communities are confident that if they build in their community, they are not going to be harmed. And unless and until they do that, I think you’re going to see, and some of our local governments have passed them, you’re going to see more and more moratoriums until people are better informed about what is coming into their community, and how they can be assured that they are going to experience the upside.

I would say, I think what’s been missing in this conversation and many others in AI and technology is that the government has not been at the table. So, you have companies that are built to make money, maybe create jobs, but make money. You have innovators, and they are built to innovate and create new things. You have a government that is supposed to be there to protect people, to protect them from the downside risks. To make sure that, as money is made, it is fair, that workers are paid a fair amount, that companies aren’t dumping pollution into the river. I mean, the government has traditionally been there to protect people when the government is running well from downside risks. The government is nowhere to be found in this space. And now you have sometimes trillion-dollar businesses, like Elon Musk, where government is not at the table, and then you have, in AI, businesses saying, “Look, we need regulation here,” and government’s still sort of like, “Whoa.”

It’s like nothing I’ve seen, and there’s this false narrative out there that I think was sort of started under Reagan, “Get government out of the way and everyone flourishes.” I think what you were seeing in this recent election, and even some of the ones before it, is a country crying out and saying, look, we need good, effective government, and we’re not feeling it. You’re not addressing our needs. We don’t feel like you’re making the change we want. It’s why I kept, as I was running, I said to people, “I’m going to address these energy costs. I’m really going to take this on because we’d seen them go up by double digits.”

Energy costs were set to go up by another double digits this year, when people were already under huge price pressures. And everyone said to me, “Oh, Mikie, everyone says that.” I’m like, “Well, first of all, I mean, you got to put me in office, and I’ll show you. But second of all,” I finally said, “Look, okay, day one, I’m freezing rate hikes. On day one, you’re going to know whether or not I’m fulfilling my commitment to you. You’re going to be able to, on day one, know where this is headed, for better or for worse.” And I did. I stopped my inaugural address, and I froze rate hikes. And since then, we’ve really expanded power generation.

We’ve taken on tough challenges, as I talked about. I mean, again and again, we are working to protect people, make their lives better, create opportunity, and innovation. In this space, because the government’s been absent, I think people are doing the only thing they have the power to do, which is just stopping it.

I’m curious about this within the framework of what the federal government can do and what the states can do. It is true that the AI CEOs would all hang out with Trump and ask to be regulated, and Trump would be like, “Go do it yourself.” And I don’t know how that worked or what anyone was thinking there. He said the agreement was morally binding, which is incredible for that cast of characters. There’s a real dynamic where you don’t want 50 different AI regulatory schemes. These are big companies, or global companies in many respects, and you do want them to innovate at a faster clip in some sort of stable or coherent national regulatory scheme.

How do you see that playing out? Because right now, a lot of what you’re describing is permitting; it’s very local, very physical, just don’t build this here, pay these utility rates. We can see that it’s very noisy, so we’ll pass some noise regulations that stop you. And the other side of it is where it’s: don’t let kids talk to chatbots like it’s their girlfriend; don’t make biological weapons with these tools… It’s harder for every state to have a patchwork of laws there. How do you connect those dots?

So, the states are a little bit the laboratories of democracy. And you’re right, I mean, good regulation at the federal level might be number one in the priority, in the good-to-bad list. We’re not getting that; that’s just not happening, probably for a couple more years. The president’s been very clear. And so, that leaves us the states. And what I think you see is a lot of these state plans coming around the same thing. I mean, we put these guardrails out earlier, but it seems to be what people are mostly coming around to, right? Community benefits, report your energy and water usage, bring your own energy, don’t raise rates on people, make sure you’re creating good jobs. So, a lot of this feels like people are coalescing around this, and you can see a world where the states operate in this way right now.

And then, as you see decent federal government, or you can even see this Congress setting something up, so the regulatory scheme is obvious, that gives businesses some understanding of where this is headed so they can get engaged. What I hope this is doing right now, and even the moratoriums, I hope what this is doing is pressuring these data centers to come up with a business model that they can sell to people. They can say to communities, I’m going to show you what it’s going to look like; I’m going to actually bring you out to one I want to build; I’m going to show you how loud it is. I’m going to show you how much water and energy usage there is, and I want you to tell me: is this going to work for your community? Does this make sense? So, I actually think this pressure could help us get a regulatory scheme that is very similar across the country.

I would also say a lot of what you’re seeing in the online space, a lot of it was the Kids Online Safety Act that the Senate passed. What, 91 people voted in favor of it in the Senate? It was very popular, but it was killed in the House when they dumped a bunch of money on Steve Scalise. So, I think what you’re seeing are these pieces of the Kids Online Safety Act, and a lot of what we’re doing, and people will start coalescing around it. New Jersey just set up the first research center in the nation, because there’s not a lot of good information for parents or teachers about what to do. And there’s all this, I would call it BS, around, oh, the social media companies, oh, we’ve given parental controls. It would be a full-time job if I wanted to keep up with the parental controls for my kids.

We do put them on; you’re constantly hearing, “Can I have more time? Can I have less?” Oh, we’re in a car ride; I’ll give you more. Oh, I forgot to take it off; now you’ve been online for eight hours. It’s not good. It’s really, really bad. This should not be dumped on parents when Big Tech has all the power here. And I sometimes hear concerns, “Well, why should we have to figure out who’s…” They know exactly who’s online, they know exactly how old you are, they can always figure it out when they want to, and they want to sell you something. But somehow, when we’re asking them, “Hey, let’s have age-appropriate design code, let’s not get compulsive or addictive behavior…” And we’re seeing that in children. I mean, the average teen spends 35 hours per week online. That’s not healthy.

That is not mentally healthy; that is not good for society, that’s not good for our kids. That’s a full-time job. They’re not connecting with other people. So, I mean, they can figure it out when they want to keep your eyes online, and what’s going to do that, but they can’t figure it out when we want to make sure we’re protecting our kids? That just doesn’t track.

I’m glad you brought up this trade-off. So many of your peers who have shown up on the show have basically offered me the formulation: “We failed to regulate social media; we will not fail to regulate AI.” That is the dynamic I’ve heard from-

So, we’re just giving up on social media?

Well, I would say we got to social media regulation 10 years later. We didn’t do it through acts of Congress. We didn’t pass a federal privacy bill. These things don’t exist. We got there through major litigation, which your state has participated in, and a bunch of state-level laws that recapitulate parts of the Kids Online Safety Act. And whenever I hear this formulation, the thing that I think is, well, it’s way easier to regulate AI because they want to build huge buildings. If there’s one thing Americans can do, it’s stop you from building huge buildings. We are good at that; we’re great at that. Maybe that’s not the right tool, but boy, are we good at swinging that hammer.

Everything about social media is speech. Everything about social media affects the First Amendment in some big and meaningful way, and we’ve never figured out how to have that conversation directly. We tend to have conversations about Section 230. We find other things that you can knock around so you don’t have to talk about, well, ultimately we are restricting how teens can speak online. And we think that’s for their benefit, and we should make that argument, but it is a speech restriction.

We’re actually not going at it as a speech restriction specifically, partly because we’ve seen this in the courts. Now, do I think that young children should be blocked from seeing hardcore porn? And do I think we should be able to restrict that? Yes. However, given some of what we’ve seen in the court cases, we are going after addictive and compulsive behavior. So, all of the algorithms that are designed to create this addictive or compulsive behavior in children, that’s what we have written the laws to address. And I think that will be very strong and resilient, and that will help address some of the First Amendment concerns that the courts are having.

And that’s the 10 years of figuring it out. Across the country, we have landed on product liability and not content moderation. The product is designed to be harmful; we’re not even going to talk about the content because then you will run into the First Amendment. There are some, I think, complications with that.

If you want to do age verification, and you want to make sure that the kids aren’t using these services when they shouldn’t be — which is part of the Meta settlement — then you’ve got to check my age too. You have to invade my privacy in some way. And the technical solution to that does not solve how I would like to be anonymous online. I have to tell Meta or the government I’m of age, and I have to produce some documentation of that.

Are you concerned about that trade-off, that as we try to protect kids by making sure they’re kids, we’re going to infringe on the rights of adults to be anonymous online?

Do you really think you’re anonymous online? I guess I don’t believe that you’re anonymous online.

Sure.

So, we’re pretending. We have this pretense that you can be anonymous online, and that they don’t know your age or that… I mean, they are tracking everything about you at all times. You just, by virtue of being online, give up this privacy. I guess I don’t quite believe that you can be anonymous online. I think that it would be very hard for them not to know everything about you and your behavior, unless you’re… Gosh, you would have to be very curated in your online experience in a way most people aren’t. But to that extent, I do worry about privacy concerns with online content because the federal government has come after a lot of our data. For example, our voter rolls, which I’ve refused to turn over, and a lot of privacy data; I’ve also seen them weaponize different personal data that they hold, including in my election against me.

So, I do worry about all this. And I think some people would suggest that I’m acting like people did about TV back in the day. Everybody acted like TV was going to be the disintegration of society. I think that there is always some adjustment period with new technologies. I do think the addictive nature of these algorithms has created a huge societal problem for children and a huge mental health problem, and I think we have to keep iterating and finding ways to address that. If there are privacy concerns, then we’re going to have to keep figuring out how to best address those and keep people’s privacy data as safe as possible.

I actually don’t think that’s a problem for this space; I think the problem is much larger than that. How do you engage online and protect your privacy, and who gets to hold that privacy data? And that’s very unclear to me. I don’t think right now anybody’s privacy is assured online. In fact, I would say quite the opposite.

Yeah, and operating from that would lead you to one set of conclusions about the legislation. Saying we should fix privacy online might lead you in another direction. I’m not sure that the big platforms want to go in that direction, right? I’m not sure they want to fix the issue of privacy. I’ll come back to that.

One of the things that’s really striking here is that New Jersey is part of the big Meta settlement; I think the state’s going to get $525 million out of that settlement. The rest of the money is unlocked if TikTok and YouTube agree to the same terms as Meta. Mark Zuckerberg is very proud of this arrangement, but Neal Mohan, the CEO of YouTube, has said YouTube is not at all interested in this. Are you going to put pressure on YouTube to agree to the same terms as Meta, or are you going to have to litigate against them too?

I assume we’ll have to litigate. We’ve just not seen anybody move in this space willingly, or kind of raise their hand, and I think they’ve learned their lesson. I think when you’ve seen people in the social media space, and you saw Facebook years ago try to move in a way that maybe made better algorithms, they just immediately lost market share to other companies. This is why I say the federal government, or any government, and state governments are so important in protecting people from the downside risks. The reason Dario Amodei has put out all of these prescriptions for regulation, and yet hasn’t unilaterally adopted them, is likely because he feels that if he did, his market share would go down, nothing would change, and everybody else would just move into that vacuum.

And so, that’s why you need the government to regulate this. Otherwise, just being a good Samaritan, a good actor in this space, doesn’t change things, and it actually harms you individually as a company.

I’m really curious about this dynamic, and I’m going to pick on Mark Zuckerberg because I love picking on Mark Zuckerberg. So, he would tell you that there should be no AI regulation; he said it out loud, and the reason is that the market will prioritize safety. If you have an AI lab and you’re going to kill everyone, people aren’t going to buy your product. This is his argument. That there is a market for this.

I know. I know it’s his argument; I just don’t buy it.

But he does not think there’s a market for social media safety, for teen safety. His settlement requires the government to pressure his competitors to agree to the same terms. I’ve heard a lot of people say that there’s no argument for safety on social media, right? But you’re a parent, I’m a parent; if you sold me an Instagram that was better for kids, I would probably say you can use that one and not TikTok.

Why do you think that market hasn’t developed? Because everyone’s asking for the government to regulate, but it seems like “this is the social media platform that’s actually safe” is a marketable product.

But it hasn’t appeared, so I assume it’s not. I assume that the money is just eyes on screens, and the safer product is not producing that. There was Kids YouTube, and I had my kid on Kids YouTube, but they gravitate towards something else, right? And so, even if you had that Instagram that was kid-friendly, and you put your kid on it, your kid would get themselves off it pretty quickly. This is why I think it’s really — I just keep coming back to it — unfair to tell parents like, “Oh, well, if you’re a good parent, you’re going to put your kid on these… We’re going to get parental controls. And if you’re a good parent, you’ll do it.” Again, I can’t tell you how many hours my husband and I have spent trying to make sure parental controls are working for our kid.

And now, the schools are just giving out laptops like candy, and my kid just goes and gets on whatever she wants to get on at school. Imagine, right? Here I am locking down her phone, and then she goes to school and can get on everything. And I’m like, I thought-

As the governor of New Jersey, you can’t make a phone call to keep the laptop out of the school? It feels like that’s a call you can make that most parents can’t.

Well, I got cell phones out of school, which my kids aren’t thanking me for, but I just got a standing ovation from teachers at the teachers’ conference. But I do think that is why we have this social media research center: what is best for children, what would the appropriate use of screens and computers be, how do you hand them out to kids, and what do you use them for? Because I’ll just tell you, to me, the canary in the coal mine was about the 2017, 2018 timeframe, when I was first running for Congress. I was speaking to people in Silicon Valley, and they were really proud to tell me that they were sending all of their children to schools without any screens. And it’s funny because that was just so foreign to me in 2018. I remember sort of thinking, like, the Amish? What are you doing?

And this is at a time when in New Jersey, we’re really proud of the fact that we’re getting every kid an iPad, right? We’re going to make sure every kid can be trained on and utilize a computer. And I think we’ve seen that those were the people developing algorithms, and those were the people that understood the brain science, how dangerous it was going to be, and making sure their kids were kept away from it. Now, we need to catch up here, but we need the data that they had, which is why we’re having this research center, so we can best understand what we can do to protect our kids.

It feels like one of the ways you would defend the sort of inevitable First Amendment lawsuit about teens and social media use is by having a bunch of data that overcomes strict scrutiny, right? You can do a proper balance of harms analysis. Is that where you’re headed? Because no one else has really tried to do that.

Yeah, that’s exactly… We have several reasons we’re doing this. We’re partly doing it to give teachers and parents good advice. When should your kid get a smartphone? I don’t know anyone who really feels like they totally know that.

My answer is never, just to be clear. My eight-year-old daughter is very upset with me because my answer is never.

I feel like that’s a great answer. Part of it is also to understand the data, because every time these social media companies have started studies, they’ve stopped them because the data is so bad. And so, that hamstrings us in lawsuits. We brought these lawsuits, and that Meta settlement was great, but we’ve lost a lot at the court level because we just don’t have the data we need. So, yes, you’re exactly right. Gathering the data and studying it so we can actually have what we need to prosecute these cases better and get better results is exactly what… That is one of the key reasons we’re doing this.

Do you think that Meta case was settled too early or for too little? I’m asking because there was a similar case in New Mexico that didn’t settle, and they won a lot more at trial. Do you think we caved too early on the Meta case?

I just think we need to keep bringing more cases. I don’t think the Meta settlement should be seen as the end of it. I think we should keep moving in this space to get better rules around it, especially given, as you’ve said, that the federal… I mean, this is another way to get kind of federal regulation to-

Right. It’s a lot of states.

And eventually the Supreme Court, to have that sort of federal standard in a way, if the government’s not going to act.

Just operationally, who makes the call and says, “We’re going to settle”? Is that a conference call? Do you have to press two to agree? How does that work?

Generally, there is a lead state in this space that kind of leads the other states in some of the litigation, and we are working closely. Our attorney general’s office works closely with the other states, and so there’s a state that is sort of the convening authority, bringing everyone together. They work together to determine, yes, this is how we’re going to move forward; this is when we think is the time to settle; we think we should pursue this; we think we should drop the case; they’ve agreed to do X, Y, and Z. So, generally, there’s a lead state that convenes everyone, and then they kind of come around to the agreement together.

This was a real dynamic in the first two years of the Trump administration. A bunch of Democratic state attorneys general said, “We’re going to do stuff because the federal government is doing nothing.” Do you think that dynamic will stay now that there’s a much more Democratic Congress?

Yeah, there’s still so much out there with HR1, with FEMA relief, with CMS… I mean, there are just tons out there still. We are still in court, litigating. We have been attacked quite a bit by the Trump administration on things like mass detention facilities and the Gateway Tunnel Project. So, we were in court very quickly there. I don’t think that will… I mean, if Trump just decides to suddenly stop, sure, but I don’t think that will be the case, unfortunately.

By the way, I’m very proud of myself for not doing the full hour on the Gateway Tunnel. I feel like there’s a great 10-episode podcast series on the twists and the turns of the Gateway Tunnel.

Oh my goodness, I am here for you. Tell me when you are ready to do that one.

It’s for another time. I want to end by talking about privacy. It has come up. It has been woven through this conversation. The notion that we don’t have any left is all over the tech industry, for a lot of reasons. And I actually think one of the things that is happening in tech and culture right now is a redefinition of privacy in very specific ways.

I’m wearing an Apple Watch right now; it has the Beta software on it, and it just makes summaries of every conversation that I have. It’s going to make one of this conversation, I’m sure. And Apple’s point of view on this is, well, it’s not a direct transcription; it is just a summary. It doesn’t identify speakers. We haven’t invaded anyone’s privacy.

There are any number of tech AI products that listen to you all day long and tell you how you feel. There’s one called the Amazon Bee that’s just come out, that you wear, and it literally listens all day long. Flock cameras exist, and Flock cameras are like a truck driven through the law that says you don’t have an expectation of privacy in public. It’s a big swirl where it’s, we’re going to take even more privacy away from you. Meta Glasses exist, and you’re like, people don’t like them, they call them pervert glasses, and Mark Zuckerberg’s entire answer is, “Well, phones don’t have a light,” and that is meant to end all conversation about the practical implications of Meta Glasses.

How do you feel about this? There are Flock cameras in New Jersey; people really don’t like feeling surveilled, and at the same time, the tech industry is rushing forward to collect even more data to feed even more AI in more and more intrusive ways. Where should we land?

I think about this all the time, and I wish I had a really great answer for you. I find it incredibly scary to think that every detail will be surveilled and that… What was it? Gattaca or Galactica? With a piece of hair that you dropped, they could do your genetic code, and then they would determine if you were in the right place because you were determined at birth to have to be in certain places or something.

That’s Gattaca.

Yeah, yeah.

The tech industry loves learning the wrong lesson from movies like this. It’s their favorite.

Oh no. But I think it’s this horrible impending sense that we are going to be so… So much is going to be known about us, that it’s going to take away our ability to thrive and live our lives. For example, you almost fear a world where, somehow, from a strand of hair, they can determine when you’re going to die and of what, and so you have to do X because you’re going to be dead by the time you’re 70. You know what I’m saying? It’s just very scary, all of the data and information, and I think what’s most scary to me is: I don’t know where it’s going and who has access to it.

I was speaking to a gentleman who was telling me about AI, and he said, “I had to give up tons of privacy, but it’s a godsend; it sorts everything out for me, it does my calendar, it reminds me to call people, it keeps my to-do list, it listens…” He said, “It is so awesome, but I had to give up a lot of privacy.” And I guess my concern wouldn’t be that if I had some system that could do that, my concern is where all this is being held, and who’s going to do something with it? When are they going to come after me because they’re like, I heard you did X, Y, and Z, or I heard you-

But this is the backlash to Flock. You’re describing in very specific ways how people feel about Flock cameras. Flock cameras are deployed by law enforcement agencies. You could change those laws today. Do you think you’re feeling the push there? Because the push there is going to connect to, okay, the FBI can subpoena my AI chat history. It’s all the same in some way.

Yeah, in some ways. I think Flock cameras are something that the communities really wanted. A couple of years ago, we had a huge outbreak in car thefts, and then everybody was having their cars stolen quite frequently. Then people were told, “Okay, lock your cars; don’t leave your key fobs in your cars.” So they stopped doing that, and they started having these break-ins in their homes, and they were very dangerous. Intruders would be in their homes while they were sleeping and stuff.

The community was very upset with law enforcement because law enforcement wasn’t ending this problem. And so, they argued for license plate readers, and law enforcement used those to track these cars and the car theft problem. Not to completely end it, but to do a lot of work there, and it seemed to have a big impact. In New Jersey, there are a lot of regulations around how long information could be kept. The attorney general audits it to make sure people aren’t using it inappropriately, et cetera, but you could still see a world where people are like, “Not good enough, I’m just going to lock down my house, and I want you to remove that camera from my street.” And those are choices that communities are making right now.

I get the tension. I get the desire to not have somebody in my home, or stealing my car, and if somebody’s going down my street and steals a car, that somebody can be caught, and that’s not threatening other people, et cetera. But I also don’t like my privacy being invaded. I don’t want everyone tracking what’s going on. Sure, you understand that they’re audited and there are all these rules, but we know some nefarious actor could break the rules. So, it is this tension, and it’s that constant thing. We could have a society where absolutely no one breaks the law. I’m sure with technology now we could monitor the hell out of everyone, and I think they do in places like Qatar.

Qatar would have you put a little app on your phone for FIFA, because we were studying all this when I was in Congress, and I was told by them, “Don’t put that app on your phone…” I didn’t go to FIFA there, but I was there to talk about one of our bases. And they said, “Don’t put that app on your phone because that’s just surveillance.” They were telling me that you can’t use your phone in your car, and if you pick up your phone, you just get a ticket because there’s that level of surveillance. Then they pointed out all the cameras to me.

That is not the surveillance state I would want to live in. So, it’s going on, and there is that tension: how much is too much? Who’s getting access to the data? That was already a problem. And now it’s not a who; it’s a what. What’s AI going to do with this data?

Right. If you link all the license plate readers together with an AI system, you can track anyone anywhere. We have supercharged the surveillance capability. That’s the thing that I’m just keyed on here at the end of this conversation because it is laced through everything else.

Everybody has had a camera on their cell phone for over a decade now, but taking all that video, putting it together through an AI system to synthesize some new reality was not a capability we had before. We didn’t have cameras on glasses, and now we have them. And again, Mark Zuckerberg’s argument is, “Phones don’t have a light,” but that means something different to people when you’re passively recording them from your glasses.

And I’m just wondering, that balance of privacy, for so long, has landed at: you don’t have an expectation of privacy in public. That is the state of the law. But you add a bunch of cameras and AI to that system, and I think people are pushing back against that law. Culturally, that expectation is changing. I should have some privacy in public.

Right. I was just thinking, though, what’s so interesting to me is, as you were talking about phones on cameras, how that has completely changed the dynamic in our understanding of police behavior, especially against certain communities of color. And I will just tell you the difference in seeing the phone videos of what was going on in communities, when police for years had been saying, “Oh, they pulled a gun,” or, “They had drugs,” or this… And the people recording it could show exactly what happened and what went down, and that was so critically important to civil rights, to criminal justice reform, and making a huge impact.

And again, that is what that tension is. What are you giving up? And you’re exactly right, the fear now is the supercharging. So, it’s not just one person’s phone. It’s like uploading all these videos, and then suddenly you have everyone being traced everywhere.

The term is sousveillance, not surveillance. We’re all going to surveil each other and put it all on Facebook, and then AI can search Facebook and find us all. This exists today. What I’m getting at, very specifically, is the idea that you have no expectation of privacy in public might be changing culturally faster than it’s changing politically or legislatively.

I’m curious if you see that balance changing state by state or at the federal level. This is the dynamic we’re in. We’re going to have little laboratories of democracy. It feels like Flock cameras are one little tick against “I have no expectation of privacy.” Actually, I want these gone. I don’t even want a license plate reader in my neighborhood because I want to feel that much less surveilled.

And you could see a world where, as we understand how AI is impacting all of these abilities, we start to create certain spaces where you do have this expectation of privacy, and say, “Look, you cannot have cameras in public parks, or you can’t have cameras in blah, blah, blah.” It’s a really difficult balance, I think. When I think about it as a woman, just about certain areas… We’re just dealing with some of the college campuses and how to keep people safe there. And as I think about removing cameras from public spaces, I also think about the concerns we have about some of the attacks on women on college campuses. Again, I just keep getting to those tension points, and I think these are just things that we have to come together as a society and say that we’re willing to accept this amount of risk, or we’re not, or we’re going to have a cop on the beat to protect people, and we’re not going to have cameras, or we are in certain dark alleys.

And that is the fear for me, though, is what you keep narrowing in on. It’s almost a little bit less about some of that, because all of that felt a little settled. It felt a little like, okay, we’re going to have some cameras out on some of these college campuses, and keep people safe. But adding that AI element takes it to a whole new, scarier level. And that’s why I think you’re saying we’re going to have to reopen these conversations.

Well, you made a face when I said my Apple Watch was recording, or summarizing —

I know, I can’t even have an Apple Watch because I can’t be looking at it every five minutes. So, I don’t do that-

Do you think that Siri feature in the Apple Watch is appropriate, where it makes summaries of all your conversations?

Again, where’s it going? Where are all these summaries going, and who’s looking at them, and why, and what are they doing with it? And are they uploading it into something? Is it anonymous? Is it not? Can they track it back to you? Who can hack into it? I mean, these are all the questions I have when I think about that. And that’s why I’m not wearing an Apple Watch.

Fair enough. Apple has a lot of technical answers to your questions. I’m curious if they will ever come up with the social answers. I have one more question for you. It is a total wild card, but I’m dying to ask you.

Oh. These are the ones that always get me. Okay, go.

New Jersey is in the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which, if enough states sign on, the presidency will be determined by the National Popular Vote winner. There are now enough new Democratic states with Democratic legislatures and Democratic governors that you could get it over the finish line. Are you going to push for that?

I’m really excited about that. I hate the Electoral College. I’ve got to tell you, I love this idea. And I was seeing some of the same reporting that you were maybe looking into. So, this is something on my mind. One day I was going to take on the Electoral College. Today might be the day, so I got to get hot on this one and see where everybody’s at because I’d love to see a popular vote.

Yeah. I’m rooting for it only because it would be a historic thing to happen in our lifetimes. But it does seem, from all of the headlines I saw after the election, I was like, oh, that is the most unlikely outcome.

You really cannot be in the most densely populated state in the nation and not want to get rid of the Electoral College. That just doesn’t make any sense. I mean, if you just care about your vote and the power of your vote.

Yeah. I think it’s a bunch of Midwest… I’m from the Midwest. There’s a bunch of Midwestern states that could sign on to it; we’ll do our best. If that happens, we’ll have you back. Actually, we should have you back to talk about privacy and all the things to come. Thank you so much, Governor Sherrill. This was great.

I really appreciate it. Thanks for having me.

Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

item.title: Robert Pattinson is Amazon’s first James Bond
item.description:
Robert Pattinson will take on the role of James Bond in Amazon MGM's first film in the 007 franchise. The next James Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve using a script written by Steven Knight, while Amy Pascal and David Heyman will produce.

The upcoming James Bond film will be the first from Amazon, which snapped up the rights to the franchise through its acquisition of MGM Studios in 2021. Amazon later gained creative control over the spy series from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson in 2025 after a years-long stalemate. item.title: Apple TV is getting video podcasts you can watch for free
item.description:
Apple's streaming service will soon have a video podcasts section, the New York Times reports. It will start testing the feature in a developer release today, so expect a new update for iOS 27.3 beta testers to roll out in a few hours. Once it rolls out fully, the new video podcasts section will be available to everyone using an Apple TV device or app on all supported platforms.

item.title: America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router
item.description:
Thirty minutes outside Atlanta, the pilot got on the intercom to announce that something was wrong.

A communications issue with the Federal Aviation Administration was cascading across the country. The pilot didn't offer much detail except to say that the issue might affect gate access and connecting flights.

For Amanda Khera, the timing couldn't be worse. Her family vacation to a small island off the coast of Belize had already turned into a medical scare when her 22-month-old son Rio developed a high fever and had to be rushed to a local clinic. Exhausted, they were trying to get home to Virginia Beach, Virginia, to see his pediatrician …
